lines.note: Funagu (船具) denotes a vessel's equipment. The Portuguese aparelhos/petrechos agrees directly; neither term requires a more specialized modern nautical interpretation.
Funaicuſa is funa-ikusa, naval warfare. Guerra por mar supplies a straightforward independent check of the Japanese compound.
Funajômǒ denotes burning a ship (船焼亡). Both marked vowels are present; the first has a circumflex and the second a caron. The kana hint deliberately does not distinguish open and closed long o.
Funamachi is waiting for a boat. Polla is the historical Portuguese contraction, not an OCR error to modernize.
Funamoto is equated with Funaba, an anchorage or port. The connector i, belongs to the explanation, not to the Japanese headword.
Completes the definition of Funamoto: the place where ships anchor. Surgem here is nautical 'come to anchor', not simply modern 'arise'.

runs.text: A percibimento que ſe faz de Fu

lines.note: Funamoyoi means preparations for a ship's departure. Enlarging the worn word supports A percibimento, with a damaged b; the repeated apercibimento below independently supports it. The separated initial A and italic Fu are retained.

runs.text: ne que eſtà pera ſe partir. ¶

lines.note: Completes italic Fu/ne, the embedded Japanese word for ship, before the Japanese example. The printed eſtà concerns a ship about to leave; do not conflate it with the headword following ¶.
Funamoyoi uo ſuru means making those preparations. The Portuguese repeats apercibimento and adds aparelho; the printed word division at a- is kept.
Completes aparelho, equipment or preparation, from the preceding physical row. It is not a new Japanese expression.
Funamuxi is a ship-associated insect, here specifically described as gnawing vessels. The Portuguese scope is narrower than simply every creature now called funamushi.
Fǔnan is wind calamity, explained as Cajeno nan (風の難). The initial caron is visible; j represents the voiced sibilant in kaze, not modern English j.
Completes the wind-calamity definition with hardship from a tempest. Trabalho has the older broader sense of trouble or suffering.
Funaqeigo is referred to the preferred Qeigobune, a guard vessel. Latin Melius introduces the preferred wording; the fleet/armada definition continues below.
Completes the fleet or naval-force gloss. This explains the collective military use of the vessel terminology rather than requiring a one-to-one modern gloss.

runs.text: Quilha do nauio por dentro, ou fun

lines.note: Funaſoco is the bottom of a vessel. The Portuguese contrasts its interior keel area with its bottom; fun continues as fundo, not the OCR fan.
Completes fundo da embarcação. The meaning confirms the preceding u without supplying an unprinted hyphen.

runs.text: Porto, ou lugar maritimo onde an-

lines.note: Funatçu denotes a harbor or maritime anchoring place. The Japanese tçu gives tsu; the Portuguese an- continues in ancorão.
Completes ancorão and names the ships as Funes. The embedded Japanese noun carries Portuguese plural s and appears italic here; retain that typeface.
Funatçuqi is a landing/anchoring place. Porto and surgidouro agree with the preceding related terms without making them duplicate entries.
Funatǒ denotes a fisherman or mariner. Restored u in Funa and the damaged letters in Peſcador/marinheiro; the faint headword mark remains less visually secure than the consonants.
Completes homem do mar, a seafaring man. It belongs to Funatǒ rather than introducing another sense of the following headword.
Funauoſa is the ship's chief (船長/船の長), also Xandô, with pilot or master as its gloss. The worn round vowel is o, not OCR e; NINJAL independently lists Funauosa.
Completes mestre do nauio. The nautical meaning supports the captain/master interpretation of Funauoſa.
Funaxu denotes a sailor or fisherman. Its xu is shu, not su; the two occupations are explicitly allowed by the Portuguese.
Funayacata is the vessel's cabin or chamber. Camara is retained without imposing a modern written accent.
Funayacu refers to offices or duties aboard a vessel. The Portuguese plural officios explains yaku as functions rather than a boat's equipment.
Funayagura is a raised ship structure, described as a sterncastle or upper deck. The definition continues with a specifically Japanese comparison.

runs.text: alto que ha nas embarcações de Iapão.

lines.note: Completes the description of a raised structure on Japanese vessels. The printed geographical name Iapão is retained.
Funayobai is calling aloud from a boat. Yobai belongs to calling here, as bradando makes clear, and should not be assigned an unrelated modern sense.
Completes embarcação from the preceding row. This short continuation has enough image context to establish its identity.

runs.text: O bulir o caualo com o corpo

lines.note: Funayurugui surprisingly describes a horse's bodily movement. The continuation explicitly compares it to a boat, so the horse reference is not an OCR semantic error.

runs.text: eſtando quedo à maneira de embarcação que eſ-

lines.note: The horse stands still while its body moves like a vessel. Quedo means stationary; preserve the seemingly paradoxical contrast between stationary position and bodily motion.
Completes the comparison with a boat rocking. This resolves the apparent mismatch between the Japanese boat compound and the horse in its gloss.
Funazoco is another form for a ship's bottom. Do not normalize its z to the ſ of Funaſoco above: both entries are present.

runs.text: O ajuntar frota de nauios, ou ẽ-

lines.note: Funazoroye is assembling a fleet. The Portuguese deliberately introduces a qualification continued below; it need not be a military fleet.

runs.text: barcações ainda que não ſeja pera guerra.

lines.note: Completes that qualification: even if not for war. The negative clause is essential to the entry's scope.
Funbari refers back to Fumbari, u. The apparent extra i came from the worn n; the scan and NINJAL support Funbari. Preserve the printed n/m difference between the two forms.

runs.text: O entender, ou diſcernir do bem, ou

lines.note: Funbet is discernment (分別), with final t representing the dictionary's syllable-final spelling. The definition begins by distinguishing good and bad.
Funbetuo curamaſu is to obscure judgment. The repeated base and surviving n/b shapes support removing OCR's spurious i from Funibetuo.
Completes Eſcurecer and starts Funbetuo midaracaſu, to disturb judgment. The physical mi- split is retained rather than joining the rows.
Completes midaracaſu and begins Fũbetuo on the next row. The nasalized Japanese abbreviation Fũ is roman throughout, not an italic final vowel.
Fũbetuo meguraſu is to turn over a matter in one's judgment. Deſcorrer com o entendimento describes reasoning; its historical initial e is retained.
Funbetni iqu, mairu, l, voyobu gives alternative ways of reaching understanding. The final vo- belongs to voyobu, not a detached object particle.

runs.text: Entender, ou alcançar com o entendi

lines.note: Completes voyobu, 'extend/reach', and the Portuguese 'understand or grasp'. No line-end hyphen is supplied merely because entendimento continues.
Funbet ſuru means to understand or discern. The enlarged final consonant supports t with its small lower terminal, not OCR r; the repeated entry supplies linguistic confirmation.
Completes the Portuguese alternative perceber. It remains a continuation of the Funbet example.
Funbetgamaxij is acting as though one possesses discernment. The -gamashii ending gives an appearance or pretension, matching the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: mento, ou que entende não ſendo aßi, ou humi

lines.note: The gloss says this appearance need not reflect actual knowledge, or may be a self-deprecating expression. Humi continues humildandoſe; the entire fragment is Portuguese italic, not Japanese mi.
Completes the self-deprecatory explanation and introduces an example with italic Vt. Dizelo de ſi means saying it of oneself.
Funbetgamaxij guinaredomo means roughly 'although it may seem a knowing matter'. The gi in gui is the historical spelling for gi, and the concessive naredomo agrees with ainda que.

runs.text: trar me ſabedor não o ſendo.

lines.note: Completes the concessive gloss: presenting oneself as knowledgeable when one is not. The first-person me should not be lost in the continuation.
Funbetxa is a discerning or knowledgeable person (分別者). The Portuguese explicitly describes good understanding.
Completes the addition '& knowledge'. This is a Portuguese continuation, not a separate headword.
Funchǔ is an insect in dung, glossed Funno muxi. The u caron is visible; the definition confirms both the dung noun and insect noun.
Completes the insect's habitat, manure. The unusual cedilla spelling of eſterço is left as the current diplomatic reading rather than modernized.
Funcot is strenuous labor (粉骨), literally Foneuo coni ſu, reducing bones to powder. This is an idiomatic intensity expression, not a literal instruction.
Funcotuo tçucuſu means exerting oneself fully. The Portuguese Tra continues trabalhar, which explains the idiom as labor or service.

runs.text: balhar, ou ſeruir com todas as forças. ¶

lines.note: Completes working or serving with all one's strength and begins abbreviated Fũcot. The nasalized fragment is Japanese roman type, not mixed italic markup.

Fũcotno côuotçumu is accumulating the merit/result of hard work. The printed Portuguese interprets it as having worked a great deal; preserve its wording rather than translating the Japanese literally into the transcription.
Completes the alternative 'having passed through many hardships'. The older participial construction is not corrected to modern grammar.
Fundô (分銅) denotes balance weights. Enlargement shows the faint circumflex missing from OCR, and the independent headword list confirms the long vowel.
Fundoxi is the loincloth. Encacho is the printed Portuguese clothing term; do not replace it with a modern familiar synonym.
Fune is a vessel. The example begins Funega moyǒ, with an alternate inflected form below; removed the artificial internal gap in Embarcação.
Moyǒta continues the mooring expression, interpreted as ships being tied together. Restored the final vowel sequence of embarcações from the scan instead of OCR embarcaçõos.
The ships are tied to one another; a new example then says Funega nagaruru, a ship drifting. The older -ruru form is retained.

runs.text: a embarcação pella agoa a baixo. ¶

lines.note: Completes the drifting-downstream gloss. The next Fune- starts another ship example and is not part of the Portuguese sentence.
Funega ſonzuru means a ship being damaged. The Portuguese includes breaking up or running against something, continued below.
Completes running ashore or onto a shoal, then begins Funega ſuuaru. Do not equate every use of Japanese 'sit' with a human posture.

runs.text: Eſtar em ſeco, ou encalhar o nauio.

lines.note: Completes ſuuaru and explains a ship being dry or aground. The physical split lacks a supplied hyphen and is retained that way.

Funega vorita, l, vyta refers to the vessel being afloat or launched. The scan really supports vorita; the Portuguese does not justify silently replacing it with another verb. Vyta is the alternative 'floated'.

runs.text: barcação, ou eſtar ja pera poder nauegar.

lines.note: Completes being ready to navigate. This fuller gloss helps explain the previous launch/afloat wording rather than requiring both Japanese alternatives to be exact synonyms.
Funeuo nauoſu is straightening or redirecting a ship. The direction sense is specified by the following Portuguese clause.

runs.text: ção, ou virala pera outro rumo. Vt,

lines.note: Virala pera outro rumo means turning it to another course. The scan supports virala, not OCR vtrala; Vt introduces a literary illustration.
Funeuo nauoxiqeruga describes having redirected the vessel, followed by waves surging against it. The connected Japanese requires reading on into vchi-cayeſarete.
Restored passive cayeſarete, 'being overturned', instead of nonsensical cayeſatete. Roman Taif. is the Taiheiki citation label; Lib. 33 is italic and the numeral is retained.

runs.text: uernarão a outro rumo, porem com as ondas ẽ-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes steering to another course but encountering contrary waves. Its historical tense spelling is preserved.

runs.text: contradas que vinhão ſendo virada, & ſoſo-

lines.note: Completes the contrary-wave clause and describes the vessel being turned and overwhelmed. The printed ſoſo- is retained as a historical spelling, not changed to modern soço-.
Completes the capsizing gloss, then Funeuo cogu means rowing the vessel. Corrected OCR Foneuo using the visible vowel and context; the embedded Fune before ¶ remains italic.
Funeuo daſu means sending the vessel out. Fazer introduces a causative Portuguese equivalent continued below.
Completes making the ship depart, then Funeni noru means boarding. The visible separation in partir a is restored; it is not the future verb partira.
Completes boarding and introduces the honorific Funeni meſaruru. The repeated maritime context does not remove the social distinction.
Completes the noble-person boarding gloss and begins Funeuo fuqimodoſu, blowing a vessel back. The f is meaningful here and should not be changed merely to long s.

runs.text: Fazer o vento arribar o nauio.

lines.note: Completes the wind-driven return: the wind causes the ship to return or put back. Arribar is understood in its nautical context.

runs.text: Febre cauſada de vento, ou ar.

lines.note: Fûnet is wind-related fever (風熱). The enlarged scan clearly shows u with circumflex, a rare but attested printed form; do not normalize it to ǔ just because that is more common.
Fungomi, u, gôda gives the verb for putting one's foot in. The example begins Cata axiuo, 'one foot'; the accent in the principal part is retained.

runs.text: ta axiuo anano nacaye fungôde iru teide

lines.note: Cata axiuo anano nacaye fungôde iru teide is having one foot in a hole. The visible mark over o points upward, agreeing with gôda above; corrected OCR caron without changing the inflection.

runs.text: Eſtaua com hum pè ja me

lines.note: Gozaru completes the Japanese expression; roman Mon. labels the wording. The Portuguese already interprets it as having one foot in the grave.

runs.text: tido na coua. i, Perto de morrer. ¶

lines.note: Completes that figurative interpretation explicitly: near death. Do- begins Doroni in the next example, not a Portuguese preposition.
Doroni fungomu is being stuck or sinking in mud. The older Japanese inflection is retained and matches atolado na lama.

runs.text: Funhoi. Cocorono gotoqu narazu. i, Fubẽ

lines.note: Funhoi is not being as one wishes, explained Cocorono gotoqu narazu and Fubẽ na coto. The nasalized e belongs to roman Japanese text; removed an accidental italic span.
Fubẽ na coto continues into the gloss of poverty or lack of necessities. The entry is broader than a narrowly modern sense of inconvenience.

runs.text: ou de poder, & habilidade pera fazer al-

lines.note: The gloss also includes lack of ability or capacity. Restored poder from the worn round vowel rather than OCR peder; no modernization of habilidade is needed.
Completes 'to do something'. The final nasalized Portuguese form remains the scan/OCR reading, not a mechanically normalized alternate tilde placement.
